title: Shop chemicals
summary: What the chemicals found in garages, hardware stores, pool sheds and salvaged devices are for, how strong the store-bought kinds are, and what each one damages. It also covers never-mix rules, rust removal, glues, PCB etching, pool chlorine for drinking water, safe storage, and first aid for splashes and fumes.

steps.text: Find the chemical in the tables and read its label before you open it: what it attacks, how strong it is, and what protection it needs.
steps.warn: Never mix chemicals. Bleach with ammonia, acids or other cleaners gives off toxic gas, and pool chlorine can start a fire if fuel, oil or other chemicals get into it.

steps.text: Work outdoors or with windows open. With flammable solvents about, keep flames and sparks away, ordinary fan motors included: only an explosion-proof fan is safe in the vapour (KS SDS alcohol). Wear goggles and gloves, and keep running water close for splashes.
Store each product closed in its original labelled container, never a drink bottle, with acids, alkalis, oxidisers such as pool chlorine, and flammables kept apart.
For a splash in the eye, flush with running water at once for at least 15 to 20 minutes, and at least 30 minutes for strong acid or lye, then follow the first-aid section.

notes:
**If help can be reached, call it first:** a poison centre or 9-1-1 for anything swallowed, in an eye, or breathed in that causes symptoms (Health Canada, WA DOH). Poison centres: Canada 1-844-764-7669 (1-844-POISON-X) (HC poison line); US 1-800-222-1222 (Poison Control caustics). Otherwise see [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_chemicals/when_no_help_is_coming).

## Never mix

| Never together | Result |
|---|---|
| Bleach + ammonia (some glass cleaners, urine) | Toxic gas; fluid in the lungs (WA DOH) |
| Bleach + any acid: vinegar, toilet bowl, rust, brick and concrete cleaners | Toxic gas (WA DOH) |
| Bleach + rubbing alcohol | Harmful fumes: dizziness, nausea, headache, loss of consciousness (NJ DOH) |
| Bleach + peroxide, acetone, anything else | Never mix household chemicals (Health Canada, Missouri Poison Center) |
| Acid + lye | Store apart; never put lye on an acid spill or acid on a lye spill (BU EHS) |
| Pool chlorine + fuel, oil, paint, acids, other pool chemicals, a splash of water | Heat, toxic gas, fire (HTH label) |
| Chlorinated brake cleaner + welding, flame, hot parts | Toxic gases, including phosgene (CCOHS fumes, CRC SDS) |

Add acid or lye **to** water, never water to them (Georgetown EHS). Add pool chemicals to plenty of water (HTH label).

## Solvents and cleaners

| Product | What you buy | Use | Watch for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Isopropyl alcohol | 99 % for electronics; 70 % rubbing alcohol is 30 % water | Boards: dries fast, no residue, safe on most plastics (MG IPA) | Flammable, flash point 12 °C (54 °F) (MG IPA) |
| Acetone | Solvent | Glue, paint, grease | Extremely flammable, flash point −18 °C (0 °F) (KS SDS acetone). Damages polycarbonate, polystyrene, acrylic (Thermo Fisher); poor on ABS, PVC (Professional Plastics) |
| Denatured alcohol | Contains methanol (KS SDS alcohol) | Fuel (KS SDS alcohol) | Toxic if swallowed, on skin or breathed in. Highly flammable, flash point 7 °C (45 °F) (KS SDS alcohol) |
| Mineral spirits | Paint thinner | Oil paint, brushes (Klean-Strip thinner); oily rust sludge (CCI) | Flammable, flash point above 38 °C (100 °F). May be fatal if swallowed and it gets into the lungs (KS SDS thinner) |
| Vinegar | At least 4.1 % acetic acid (FDR) | Rust soak (CRC) | An acid: never with bleach |
| Washing soda | Sodium carbonate | Cleaning, electrolysis | Not on aluminium or fibreglass (Arm & Hammer) |
| Brake cleaner, chlorinated | Over 95 % tetrachloroethylene in the CRC Brakleen SDS of 2010; check your own label (CRC SDS) | Degreasing | Never near welding or heat (CRC SDS), or weld parts still wet with it (CCOHS fumes). Keep it away from strong bases and strong oxidisers such as pool chlorine (CRC SDS) |

## Rust removal and metal prep

| Method | How | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Steel wool and oil | 000 or 0000 wool, a few drops of light oil, wipe with mineral spirits; for thin, even rust only (CCI) | Bare metal re-rusts (CCI) |
| Vinegar | Soak 12 to 24 h (CRC) | Too long harms the tool (CRC) |
| Molasses | About 10 parts water to 1; one museum example took 2 weeks (CMF) | Slow |
| Phosphoric acid gel (Naval Jelly) | Apply at 10 to 32 °C (50 to 90 °F), leave 5 to 10 min, never over 15, rinse with water, coat or paint within 24 h (Henkel Naval Jelly) | Iron and steel only: not aluminium, chrome, stainless, cement, fibreglass, marble, plastic or paint; it strips paint, so wipe it off painted surfaces at once (Henkel Naval Jelly) |
| Rust converter (phosphoric acid, tannin) | Leaves a dark protective film (Texas A&M CRL) | Tannin isn't a permanent coating (CCI) |

**Electrolysis:** a plastic tub, 1 tablespoon washing soda per 3.8 L (1 US gal) of water (CRC); conservators use 5 % (Texas A&M CRL). Rusty part to negative (black), scrap mild steel to positive (red) (CRC, Texas A&M CRL). **Never stainless steel** as the sacrificial metal (CRC). Low-voltage DC: conservators rarely go above 6 V, while CRC's own method uses a 12 V charger. Battery chargers are not made for this and can overheat (Texas A&M CRL). It gives off hydrogen and caustic mist: work outdoors or exhaust it (Texas A&M CRL). Hydrogen is extremely flammable: keep flames and sparks away (Exide SDS).

Then dry and oil or paint at once (CRC). Keep iron at 50 % relative humidity or less, and below 35 % if it is still rusting (CCI).

## Acids and alkalis

| Chemical | Where, how strong | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| Battery acid (sulfuric) | Flooded lead-acid batteries, 30 to 40 % (Exide SDS) | Top up after charging with distilled or de-ionised water only, to 3 mm (1/8 in) below the vent well. Never add acid (Trojan). Batteries give off flammable hydrogen: keep flames and sparks away and don't bridge the terminals (Exide SDS) |
| Muriatic acid (hydrochloric) | Pool and masonry aisles (EPA pool alert, WA DOH), about 31 % (Multi-Blend SDS) | Corrodes most metals (NIOSH HCl): keep it away from tools. Ventilate (Multi-Blend SDS) |
| Lye (sodium hydroxide) | Crystal drain openers, 96 to 100 % (Roebic SDS) | Attacks aluminium, tin, zinc (NIOSH NaOH). Gets hot in water (Roebic SDS) |
| Hydrofluoric acid | Some rust-stain removers (Poison Control laundry) | **Avoid.** Skin may look only red while damage is severe, and body-wide harm can follow up to 24 h later (KU Poison) |

## Lye from wood ash

Water dripped through wood ash gives a brown lye that makes soft soap (Troup History). Wear goggles, gloves and long sleeves; keep children and pets away (Soap Queen safety). Splashes: [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_chemicals/when_no_help_is_coming). Use plenty of running water, never vinegar, which adds heat (Soap Queen safety), and keep flushing a long time: for lye (sodium hydroxide) CCOHS says 60 min (CCOHS lye).

**Ash:** hardwood such as hickory, sugar maple, beech or oak, as softwood ash gives weaker lye (Classic Bells ash, MEN ashes, Countryside), kept dry as rain washes the potassium out (MU ash), in a lidded metal can outdoors, at least 3 m (10 ft) from the house (USFA). Never ash from trash, cardboard, coal, barbecue charcoal, or painted, stained or treated wood (OSU ash), nor wood of unknown origin (UW ash).

**Containers:** never aluminium, tin, galvanised zinc, magnesium, chromium, brass or bronze: lye gives off explosive hydrogen with them (Certified Lye). Lye etches enamel; heat it in stainless steel (MEN soft soap), but stainless alloys vary and unmarked pots may not stand it (Classic Bells containers). Collect it in glass, ceramic or HDPE plastic, but store it only in HDPE (code 2) or PP (code 5) plastic: lye etches and weakens glass, and cracks PET soda bottles (Fort Scott, Certified Lye, Classic Bells containers). Keep it closed and labelled LYE (Certified Lye, Soap Queen safety).

| Step | How |
|---|---|
| Hopper | Wooden barrel or HDPE bucket with holes, raised over a glass, ceramic or HDPE vessel (not aluminium or galvanised): gravel, straw, twigs, then packed ash (Countryside, MEN ashes, Fort Scott, Certified Lye) |
| Water | Rainwater (Countryside), 3.8 L (1 US gal) every hour or two for a day or more (Child), each lot once the last has soaked in (MEN ashes) |
| Strengthen | Re-run through fresh ash (Child), or boil down outdoors in stainless steel until it passes the egg test, often to a quarter of the volume (MEN soft soap), as the fumes are harmful (Sutter's Fort, Soap Queen safety) |

| Test | Means |
|---|---|
| Egg or potato sinks | Too weak (Child) |
| Shows a small patch, as big as a ninepence (an old small coin) | Right for soap (Child) |
| Floats half out | Too strong: add rainwater (Child, Countryside) |
| Chicken feather dissolves | Strong enough (Countryside) |
| pH paper | Not a strength test: pH barely moves as lye gets stronger (Classic Bells ash). One writer reports about 11 for drip lye and 14 for bought lye (MEN soft soap). Ash lye is very caustic (Countryside) |

Float tests are rough and sources differ: MEN soft soap floats the egg mid-liquid for mild soap and a quarter out for laundry soap, Classic Bells accepts about half out. Old eggs float higher (Classic Bells ash). Too weak gives no soap; too strong gives harsh soap (Child, Countryside), so aim low and check the finished soap.

**Fat:** tallow, lard or used cooking grease (Fort Scott, Countryside). To clean it, boil it with water, cool overnight and lift off the fat on top (Sutter's Fort).

**Soap:** 0.9 kg (2 lb) fat per 3.8 L (1 US gal) of lye (Fort Scott), for ash lye that passes the egg test (MEN soft soap). Old recipes run from equal parts fat and lye to 1 part fat to 3 of lye (Countryside, MEN soft soap), so it is only a start. For bought lye, use a lye calculator (Countryside). Boil outdoors in a stainless steel kettle (MEN soft soap) no more than half full (MEN ashes), 45 min to 8 h until thick (Fort Scott, Sutter's Fort). Done when thick and ropy (Child), glossy like petroleum jelly; it stays soft (MEN soft soap). For bars, stir in 1.2 L (2½ US pints) of salt per 19 L (5 US gal) of tallow (about 60 mL, ¼ cup, per 0.9 kg or 2 lb of fat) as you pour into a wooden mould (MEN ashes, Troup History); let it set up to a week, then cut (Fort Scott).

**Safe to use?** Too much lye or too short a cure makes soap harsh (DAR Museum). After 5 days, touch a pH strip to its lather: 9 to 10 is normal, 11 to 12 is lye heavy but fine for laundry, 13 to 14 only for dirty rags (Soap Queen lye-heavy). Throw out soap that separated or has lye pockets, gloved and double-bagged (Soap Queen lye-heavy).

**Cleaning:** first-run lye cuts grease (MEN ashes); soak dirty clothes overnight in weak lye water, then drain, soap, rub and rinse (Sutter's Fort); keep gloves on (Soap Queen safety); soft soap for floors, hard for clothes (Child).

## Pool chlorine for drinking water

Use only **plain unscented bleach** or **plain granular calcium hypochlorite** ("HTH", at least 70 % available chlorine) (HTH label). Health Canada gives only a liquid bleach method: 2 drops (0.2 mL) of unscented 5.25 % household bleach per litre (4 cups) of water, stirred and left 30 min (HC emergency). Stabilised pool tablets (trichlor, dichlor) and products with algaecide or clarifier are in neither the EPA nor the Health Canada method: don't drink water treated with them. EPA does allow water-disinfection tablets made for the purpose, used to their own label (EPA water). Health Canada's well page says not to use swimming pool or hot tub disinfectants, as they hold other chemicals (HC well).

EPA method: settle and filter cloudy water. Stir 1 heaping teaspoon (about 7 g) of HTH into 7.6 L (2 US gal) of water until dissolved, with ventilation, eye protection and rubber gloves (EPA water, HTH label). Don't store the stock: the HTH label says to use the solution as soon as it is mixed. Add 1 part of this stock to 100 parts water, 10 mL per litre (EPA water; metric converted from its US units). Wait 30 min, as EPA gives for bleach: the water should smell slightly of chlorine. If it doesn't, add the same dose again and wait 15 min more (EPA water, HTH label). Smell is only a rough check, since noses differ (Health Canada chlorine TD). A pool or spa test kit that reads free chlorine (a DPD kit, not an OTO kit; San Bernardino pool kit) is better: aim for at least 0.5 mg/L after the 30-minute wait on a treated batch (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO), and wait longer if the water is cold (WHO chlorine test). See [Test water with found kits](#guides/test_water). Bleach weakens with age and heat: use bleach that is fresh or under a year old at room temperature (EPA water), and test and raise the dose if it has aged (EPA bleach label). Chlorine won't remove heavy metals, salts or most chemicals (EPA water). More in [Sanitation](#ref/reference_sanitation/keep_drinking_water_separate) and [Water filters](#ref/reference_water_filters/if_the_water_is_doubtful).

## Joining and fixing

**Flux:** acid (chloride) flux is corrosive, conducts and is hard to wash out: **never on electronics**. Use rosin flux (NEETS).

| Glue | Joins | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| Epoxy | Most materials; cures in thick sections (Henkel plastics) | Exact mix; slow; big batches get hot |
| Super glue | Close-fitting small parts | Poor peel, gaps, heat (Henkel plastics) |
| PVC / ABS cement | PVC to PVC, ABS to ABS; green transition cement for ABS to PVC, non-pressure (Oatey) | Primer on PVC, never ABS (Oatey) |
| Silicone | Flexible seals | Weak. Acetoxy (vinegar-smelling) kinds give off acetic acid and can corrode electronics. Alkoxy cure is non-corrosive and suits electronics; oxime cure can stain copper or brass (Henkel plastics) |
| Polyurethane | Very tough (Henkel plastics) | One-part cures only about 9.5 mm (3/8 in) deep |
| Contact cement | Laminate, rubber, leather to wood or metal: coat both, dry 15 to 20 min, press (DAP) | No repositioning. Not structural, copper or polystyrene foam. Solvent-based and very flammable, flash point about −6 °C (21 °F) (DAP) |
| Hot glue | Plastics | Poor on metals (Henkel plastics) |

**Polyethylene and polypropylene** barely glue without a polyolefin primer or polyolefin hot melt (Henkel plastics).

| Threadlocker | Strength | To undo |
|---|---|---|
| Purple 222 | Low, small screws | Hand tools (Loctite 222) |
| Blue 242 | Medium | Hand tools. Only if they fail: heat the nut or bolt itself to about 250 °C (482 °F) and undo it while hot (Loctite 242) |
| Red 271 | High, permanent | Heat the nut or bolt itself to about 250 °C (482 °F) and undo it while hot (Loctite 271) |
| Green 290 | Medium to high; wicks into assembled threads | Hand tools; in rare cases heat the nut or bolt itself to about 250 °C (482 °F) (Loctite 290) |

## Keeping things dry and clean

- **Silica gel:** blue turns pink, then white when full; blue contains toxic cobalt chloride, keep it from food (Ted Pella, AGM). Orange turns green (AGM). Recharge loose gel at no more than 130 °C (266 °F) until the colour returns: some gel gives off toxic fumes if overheated (AGM). Above 162 °C (325 °F) ruins it. Don't microwave packaged desiccant (Ted Pella).
- **Calcium chloride** tubs (about 78 %) pull water from the air into brine (DampRid label, OxyChem). Keep the brine off metal and leather. The product irritates eyes and skin and is harmful if swallowed: keep it from children (DampRid label).
- **Activated carbon** removes chlorine taste, odours and many organic chemicals. It does **not** make water germ-free (use it after disinfecting), nor remove iron, fluoride, sodium or nitrate. Change it: old carbon grows bacteria (Alberta Agriculture, MDH).

## PCB etching

| | Ferric chloride | Sodium persulfate |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | Ready to use, about 38 % (MG ferric chloride) | 250 g per litre of water (MG prototyping) |
| Warm to | 35 to 55 °C, never above 55 °C (131 °F) (MG ferric chloride) | 50 °C (122 °F) (MG prototyping) |
| Keep in | Plastic, never metal (MG ferric chloride) | Vented plastic or glass: it gives off gas (MG prototyping) |

Wear goggles and gloves. **Spent etchant holds copper, highly toxic to aquatic life: never down a drain or onto the ground.** Take it to hazardous waste with the SDS (MG prototyping, MG ferric chloride). For ferric chloride MG also allows: add washing soda until pH paper reads 7 to 8, let the copper settle, and bag the sludge for disposal under local rules (MG 415 page).

## Storage and spills

- Original labelled container, closed, locked from children; never a drink bottle (Health Canada child safety).
- Keep acids, bases, oxidisers and flammables apart (Georgetown EHS). Pool chlorine is an oxidiser (EPA pool alert): dry, off the floor, away from gasoline, oil, paint solvents, oily rags and ignition sources (EPA pool alert); don't mix old and new product, even of the same type (EPA pool alert).
- Avoid temperature swings (Health Canada). Label ranges: IPA −20 to 27 °C, ferric chloride 16 to 27 °C, threadlocker 8 to 21 °C (MG IPA, MG ferric chloride, Loctite 242).
- **Small spill:** gloves and goggles; if flammable, no flames or sparks; ventilate. Cover with absorbent or cat litter, sweep from the edges in, bag it. Baking soda on small acid spills (UC ANR). Never use sawdust, paper, rags, wood or paper cat litter or other organic matter on an oxidiser such as pool chlorine: it can ignite (CCOHS spills, HTH label). Scoop pool chlorine with a clean, dry metal or plastic utensil into a separate container, never back into the tub, and don't sweep fine powder into the air (HTH label, EPA pool alert, CCOHS spills). Unsure? Leave and get help (CCOHS spills).

## When no help is coming

**Eye:** flush at once with lukewarm running water, lids open, for at least 15 to 20 minutes; remove contacts without delaying (Poison Control eye, CCOHS eyewash). Strong acid or lye: at least 30 minutes, until help arrives; alkali burns tend to be worse (Merck Manual).

**Skin:** remove soaked clothing and rinse at least 20 minutes (Poison Control caustics).

**Swallowed:** don't make them vomit. Rinse the mouth, then a small drink of water (Multi-Blend SDS, Poison Control caustics). Fuel, solvent or mineral spirits: see [Vehicles](#ref/reference_vehicles/when_no_help_is_coming). Nothing by mouth, not even water, if unconscious, having convulsions or unable to swallow (Roebic SDS).

**Fumes:** fresh air (CRC SDS). After chlorine or ammonia fumes, lung damage can appear or worsen later: after chlorine, fluid in the lungs can be delayed up to 24 hours and symptoms for days (NIOSH chlorine); ammonia injury can keep worsening for 18 to 24 hours (ATSDR ammonia). Watch the person for at least a day.

**Beyond first aid:** an eye still painful or blurry an hour after you started flushing, any HF contact, a swallowed corrosive with throat or chest pain, or breathing that worsens. These need a hospital (Poison Control eye, KU Poison, Poison Control caustics, NIOSH chlorine).
